secs.t: SI base units, dimensions and definitions · Revision points (10)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #5 (pp 10-14), #6 (pp 14-17)
The
mole
is the SI unit of amount of substance.
Three are SI base units: metre, ampere and kelvin.
Length is in metres, mass in kilograms, time in seconds, and power in watts.
The dimension symbol for length is L.
Temperature uses Θ (kelvin), amount of substance N (mole), and luminous intensity J (candela).
Since 2019 the metre is fixed by the speed of light, the kelvin by the Boltzmann constant, and the candela by a luminous efficacy of 683 lm/W at 540 THz.
Since 2019 the ampere is defined by fixing the elementary charge at 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Planck's constant fixes the kilogram, Boltzmann's the kelvin, and Avogadro's the mole.
The SI standard for time is the second.
The mole is defined using the fixed Avogadro constant N_A = 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
The kilogram is defined using the fixed value of Planck constant h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

secs.t: Derived SI units · Revision points (7)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #5 (pp 10-14)
One standard atmosphere is
The unit of force is newton (N).
The SI unit of capacitance is farad (F).
The henry measures inductance, the weber magnetic flux, the tesla magnetic field, and the farad capacitance.
Energy (joule) is kg m² s⁻², power (watt) kg m² s⁻³, pressure (pascal) kg m⁻¹ s⁻², and charge (coulomb) A s.
Potential difference (volt) is kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹, resistance (ohm) kg m² s⁻³ A⁻², frequency (hertz) s⁻¹, and charge A s.
Potential difference or electromotive force is measured in volts (V).

secs.t: Conversions and extremes of scale · Revision points (9)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #5 (pp 10-14)
1 bar is exactly 10⁵ Pa.
One micrometre equals 10⁻⁶ metres.
1 km = 10³ m, 1 cm = 10⁻² m, 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, and 1 AU ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m.
1 g = 10⁻³ kg, 1 hour = 3600 s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and 1 calorie = 4.186 J.
One erg (the CGS unit of energy) equals 10⁻⁷ J. 10⁻⁵ N is one dyne.
The theoretical smallest practical unit of length is Planck length, approximately 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ metres.
Quecto means 10⁻³⁰, the elementary charge is about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, quetta means 10³⁰, and the observable universe is about 10²⁶ m across.
Two are astronomical mass units: solar mass and galactic mass.
The LHC works at the TeV (tera-electronvolt) energy scale.

secs.t: Measuring instruments · Revision points (15)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #6 (pp 14-17)
A
galvanometer
detects or measures small currents.
A screw gauge works on the pitch of the screw and a circular scale.
A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.
A screw gauge measures thin wires or sheets, an optical bench focal lengths, a resonance tube the speed of sound in air, and a spectrometer refractive index and wavelength.
A potentiometer is used for emf comparison.
Three are used for length: main plus Vernier scale, pitch plus circular scale, and a plain linear scale.
Vernier calipers measure external diameter, a clock measures time, a spring balance measures force, and a beam balance measures mass.
Vernier calipers measure internal diameter and depth, a spring balance measures weight, and a thermometer measures temperature.
A manometer measures pressure difference, a sextant angles in navigation, a spectrometer spectra, and Vernier calipers objects up to about 15–30 cm.
A screw gauge has a least count of
The metre bridge and post-office box measure resistance, a potentiometer uses null deflection, and ammeters and voltmeters work on the magnetic effect of current.
An ammeter or voltmeter uses a moving coil.
A galvanometer works on the torque on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field.
A metre scale is marked in metres, centimetres and millimetres.
The Celsius scale uses °C, the Kelvin scale K, and the Fahrenheit scale °F.

secs.t: Force and its types · Revision points (10)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #14 (pp 38-44)
Centripetal force
acts towards the centre and keeps a body on a circular path.
Force is measured in
newton
s (N).
An unbalanced force changes the state of motion.
Frictional force opposes relative motion or the tendency of motion.
Gravitational force attracts objects towards each other.
The dyne is another unit of force.
All five can supply centripetal force: tension (stone on string), gravity (satellite), friction (car on curve), electrostatic (electron) and magnetic force (charged particle in a field).
The second law is
F = ma
: force equals mass times acceleration.
A balanced force causes no change in an object's state of motion.
Friction converts kinetic energy to heat during vehicle braking.

secs.t: Newton's laws and momentum · Revision points (11)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #14 (pp 38-44)
Rocket propulsion
is Newton's third law: gases are pushed backward and the rocket is pushed forward.
Sudden braking effects demonstrate Newton's first law.
Airbags increase the time of impact and decrease force.
Rocket gases push down and the rocket moves up.
Rest until pushed is the first law, the heavy suitcase and loaded cart show F = ma (second law), and rocket gases show the third law.
A foot pushes the ground backward.
The gun recoils backward.
The force on the Earth equals the force on the apple, but the Earth's huge mass makes its acceleration
very small
, not zero.
Without external force an isolated system's momentum is conserved in every collision, and an explosion from rest keeps total momentum zero.
Vehicle safety design uses collision principles.
A longer impact time means a smaller force for the same momentum change (second law).

secs.t: Work, energy and power · Revision points (11)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #14 (pp 38-44)
One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves a body 1 metre, so
1 J = 1 N m
One horsepower equals
atts.
Mechanical energy conservation is expressed as KE + PE = constant.
Mechanical energy is KE + PE, thermal energy comes from molecular motion, KE can be translational or rotational, and PE can be gravitational or elastic.
A generator turns mechanical into electrical, a motor electrical into mechanical, a battery chemical into electrical and a solar cell light into electrical energy.
The SI unit of work is the joule (J).
Sound, light, electrical, magnetic and nuclear are energy forms, an LED turns electrical into light, and a nuclear plant turns nuclear into heat then electricity.
All three convert potential into kinetic energy: a falling body, a swinging pendulum and a roller coaster going down.
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed.
All four show conservation of mechanical energy: a pendulum, free fall, a spring-mass system and ideal (elastic) collisions.
The SI unit of power is the watt (W).

secs.t: Friction · Revision points (8)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #14 (pp 38-44)
Fluid friction (viscous drag) opposes motion through fluids, it does not assist it.
Friction converts kinetic energy to heat during vehicle braking.
Three are advantages: walking, moving and stopping vehicles, and writing or holding.
Static friction is self-adjusting.
Friction is necessary for forward push during walking and running.
All four are disadvantages of friction: unwanted heat, lower machine efficiency, extra fuel use and surfaces wearing rough over time.
Friction produces heat to ignite a matchstick.
Without friction, people slip.

secs.t: Circular motion and simple machines · Revision points (7)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #14 (pp 38-44)
Friction provides centripetal force for a vehicle on a level circular road.
A lever is used in scissors.
Gravity and normal force provide centripetal force in a loop-the-loop.
Water is thrown outward in a washing machine.
Gears convert speed or torque, as in bicycles, clocks and cars.
Pulleys lift loads in cranes, flagpoles and elevators, and gears are used in bicycles, clocks and automobiles.
The crowbar, bottle opener and human forearm are levers, and the screwdriver is a wheel and axle.

secs.t: Gravity and the value of g · Revision points (14)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #23 (pp 96-98)
Weight is the force with which the Earth attracts a body.
The Earth is not perfectly spherical but slightly oblate, bulging at the equator because of rotation and gravity.
Gravity holds gases near the planet, an effect called
atmosphere retention
All bodies fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum, independent of mass.
Acceleration due to gravity always points towards the centre of the Earth, which is why things fall straight down.
The value of g is maximum at the poles and minimum at the equator.
The poles have zero centrifugal force.
Three are linked to zero weight: the Earth's centre, very great height and a freely falling lift.
Orbital motion keeps planets and satellites in orbit.
At very large height, g approaches zero.
Weight is greatest at the Earth's surface; it falls going up, going down and in far space, and is zero at the Earth's centre.
Microgravity experiments study
human physiology
, along with fluid behaviour and crystal growth.
Ignoring air resistance, every freely falling body accelerates at g, about 9.8 m s⁻², whatever its mass.
The equator
is the point on the surface farthest from the Earth's centre because of the equatorial bulge of the oblate Earth.

secs.t: Mass, weight and weightlessness · Revision points (8)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #23 (pp 96-98)
Weight is mass times gravitational acceleration,
W = mg
, so it is measured in newtons.
Mass represents inertia or the amount of matter.
Apparent weight is zero inside an orbiting satellite.
At the centre of Earth, g equals zero.
Zero-g training
uses aircraft flying parabolic paths, which give astronauts short spells of free fall.
Astronauts in space stations are in continuous free fall, microgravity is used to study fluids, crystals and physiology, and satellite instruments are built for weightlessness.
Weight is in newtons, mass is in kilograms, and weight can vanish in weightlessness while mass stays the same.
All four reduce weight: height above the surface, depth below it, the Moon (about one-sixth) and far space where it nears zero.

; the ISS sits near 400 km.

400 km

secs.t: Density, buoyancy and Pascal's law · Revision points (10)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #22 (pp 92-96)
An object floats when its density is less than the liquid’s density.
Atmospheric density decreases with height.
Hydraulic brakes transmit pressure equally to all wheels.
Pressure rises with depth, so the bottom of a submerged body is pushed harder than its top.
Ships and boats float when their weight equals the buoyant force.
All five use Archimedes' principle: ships, submarines, balloons and airships, hydrometers and lactometers, and life jackets.
Buoyant force acts
vertically upward through the centre of buoyancy
, the centre of the displaced liquid.

A hydraulic jack lifts vehicles, excavators move arms and buckets with hydraulic cylinders, a hydraulic press compresses bales and presses sheets, and hydraulic brakes pass pressure equally to all wheels.
A hydrometer measures liquid density, a lactometer checks milk purity, and life jackets increase buoyant force.
Only a small part of an iceberg remains above water.

secs.t: Surface tension and capillarity · Revision points (8)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #22 (pp 92-96)

A water strider walks on the surface acting as an elastic membrane, small drops are spherical to minimise area, detergent lowers surface tension to improve wetting, and soap bubbles have two surfaces with higher excess pressure.
Detergents reduce surface tension.
Water rises in a narrow glass tube with a concave meniscus.
All four are capillary action: oil rising in a wick, damp rising in walls, water rising in plants and ink soaking into blotting paper.
The contact angle in wetting depends on surface tension.
Water rises in plants by capillarity, lung surfactants lower surface tension, molten metal forms spheres in space, and droppers and pens rely on drop formation.
Mercury forms a convex meniscus and is depressed in a glass tube, because its cohesion is stronger than its adhesion to glass.
Cranes use steel cables with high Young’s modulus.

secs.t: Viscosity, elasticity and compressibility · Revision points (7)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #22 (pp 92-96)
Viscous oils lubricate machines, streamlining cuts drag, viscosity affects blood flow, and raindrops and parachutes reach terminal velocity.
Springs store elastic energy.
Submarine hulls must withstand high pressure.
Hydraulic shock absorbers use viscous damping.
Bridges and buildings use materials selected for high elasticity or strength.
Liquids suit hydraulics because they barely compress, air's compressibility cushions pneumatic absorbers, and bulk modulus contrasts liquids with gases.
Gases are highly compressible, so large amounts can be squeezed into cylinders.

secs.t: Heat, temperature and scales · Revision points (11)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #21 (pp 86-92)
Heat is energy in transit that flows because of a temperature difference, from hot to cold.
Heat supplied is Q = m c ΔT, so it depends on mass, specific heat and the change in temperature.
The SI unit of heat or energy is the joule (J).
The Celsius scale has an ice point of 0°C.
The Kelvin temperature is equal to the Celsius temperature plus 273.15.
Absolute zero is 0 K, –273.15°C and –459.67°F, and it is the zero point of the Kelvin scale.
Temperature measures how hot or cold a body is and reflects the average kinetic energy of its molecules.
Bodies at the same temperature are in thermal equilibrium, so no net heat flows between them.
Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature.
The symbol of the Fahrenheit scale is °F.
Heat flows from a higher temperature to a lower temperature.

secs.t: Transfer of heat · Revision points (8)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #21 (pp 86-92)
Conduction transfers heat through direct contact.
Conduction passes heat particle to particle without bulk motion, convection needs a fluid, radiation can cross a vacuum, and a vacuum flask is built to cut all three.
Heat travels along the metal from particle to particle by conduction.
Shiny walls reflect radiant heat and cut losses in a thermos.

In boiling water hot water rises and cold sinks, breezes arise from unequal heating of land and sea, heaters and air conditioners set up convection currents in a room, and a balloon rises because heated air is lighter.
The Sun's heat reaches the Earth through the vacuum of space by radiation.
A metal base conducts heat quickly from the flame to the food, so utensils are made of good conductors.
Wood and plastic provide insulation because they are poor conductors.

secs.t: Thermal expansion and the anomaly of water · Revision points (5)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #21 (pp 86-92)
Railway tracks have gaps left for thermal expansion.
Water contracts when heated from 0°C to 4°C.
The density of water decreases below 4°C.
Liquids expand when heated, so tanks have overflow pipes to let the extra volume escape safely.
Thermometers use liquid expansion to measure temperature.

secs.t: Specific heat and latent heat · Revision points (9)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #21 (pp 86-92)
Water is used as a coolant because its high specific heat allows it to absorb large heat with a small temperature change.
The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg.
Raising the pressure raises the boiling point, which is why a pressure cooker cooks faster.
Coastal areas have a moderate climate because of the high specific heat of water.
All four involve latent heat: ice absorbs it on melting, steam releases extra heat in burns, sweat absorbs it when evaporating, and condensation releases it in clouds.
Temperature stays fixed while ice melts because the heat goes into latent heat.
Liquid refrigerant evaporates at low pressure.
The refrigerant absorbs heat inside the fridge as it evaporates and gives it out at the back as it condenses.
A refrigerator extracts heat from the cold body inside and rejects heat to the hot surroundings.

secs.t: Evaporation, refrigeration and heat engines · Revision points (10)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #21 (pp 86-92)
Evaporation is a surface process at any temperature, it speeds up with heat, area, wind and low humidity, and losing fast molecules cools the liquid.
Inside the freezer the refrigerant evaporates and absorbs heat; it is then compressed, condenses and gives out heat outside, and finally expands through a valve.
Ammonia was an earlier refrigerant.
A refrigerator extracts heat from the cold body inside and rejects heat to the hot surroundings.
A heat engine converts heat energy into mechanical work.
Three show evaporative cooling: sweating, the earthen pot and desert coolers.
A heat engine is based on the First Law and Second Law of Thermodynamics.
R-134a (an HFC) and R-600a (isobutane, an HC) are modern refrigerants.
All four are desired: a low boiling point, high latent heat, non-toxicity and stability, along with non-flammability.
Freons are CFCs.

secs.t: Types of waves · Revision points (13)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #20 (pp 81-86)
Matter waves belong to moving particles such as electrons and need no material medium.
Sound waves in air are longitudinal waves.
Radio waves have wavelengths greater than 1 metre.
Visible light
spans about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red).
Matter waves
are associated with de Broglie.
Shock waves, like matter waves, fall under "
other classification
", not under dimension, medium or direction of vibration.
Waves in a spring
such as a slinky can be either longitudinal or transverse.
Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths, below about 0.01 nm.
Light waves are electromagnetic waves.
S-waves are secondary and P-waves primary seismic waves, and all electromagnetic waves are transverse.
P-waves travel through solids, liquids, and gases.
Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave that needs a medium, so it cannot cross a vacuum.
Sound travels as compressions and rarefactions, and without a medium its speed is zero, so it cannot travel in a vacuum.

secs.t: Wave properties, energy and uses · Revision points (11)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #20 (pp 81-86)
Larger amplitude means louder sound or brighter light.
Velocity is independent of frequency in the same medium.
At the same frequency, higher velocity produces a longer wavelength.
Wave energy depends on both amplitude squared and frequency squared, not on frequency alone.
Radio waves are used in mobile communication.
Waves transfer energy without transferring matter.
Sound is used in sonar, radio in broadcasting, X-rays in security scanning and ultrasound in ranging.
Light waves are used in optical fibres.
Microwaves are used for cooking.
Ultrasonic waves are used for
cleaning
, echocardiography and ranging.
Loudness is the sensation of intensity or amplitude.

secs.t: Interference, diffraction, polarization and Doppler effect · Revision points (15)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #20 (pp 81-86), #19 (pp 76-81)
Young’s double-slit experiment demonstrates constructive and destructive interference of light.
Noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference of sound.
Sound can be heard around corners because sound waves diffract easily.
Polaroid sunglasses reduce glare by cutting reflected light.
Medical Doppler ultrasound
measures blood-flow speed from the frequency shift of echoes.
Bending of light around an obstacle allows light to enter the geometrical shadow.
All four use polarisation: Polaroid sunglasses, 3D movie glasses, LCD screens and optical activity to measure solution concentration.
All four use the Doppler effect: radar speed guns, medical ultrasound, weather radar and bat echolocation, each measuring a frequency shift.
Photoelasticity
uses polarised light to reveal stress patterns in transparent models.
Astronomy uses red shift and blue shift to study the expanding universe and star motion.
Photography uses glare-reduction filters.
SONAR measures the speed of submarines and underwater objects using the Doppler effect.
Higher frequency produces higher pitch.
The Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency due to relative motion between a source and an observer.
Sirens demonstrate the Doppler effect.

secs.t: Sound — nature, speed and characteristics · Revision points (19)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #19 (pp 76-81)
Sound in glass travels about 5000–6000 m/s like other solids, not at air's 340 m/s.
Amplitude determines the loudness of sound.
The human audible frequency range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Using λ = v/f, 340 ÷ 20 =
The distance between two successive compressions is the wavelength.
The speed of sound increases with an increase in temperature.
Frequency is vibrations or compressions per second, measured in hertz, and it sets the pitch.
Higher frequency corresponds to smaller wavelength.
Low frequency produces a bass or deep sound.
Pitch is directly proportional to frequency
: higher frequency is heard as higher pitch.
Quality or timbre distinguishes two sounds having the same pitch and loudness.
Quality or timbre depends on the harmonics present.
The speed of sound at 0°C is approximately 331 m/s.
The speed of sound is generally greatest in solids.
Sound travels at an intermediate speed through liquids.
Humans hear up to about 20 kHz, and this upper limit falls with age, with the loss most marked at high frequencies.
Loudness is measured in decibels (dB).
Sound requires a material medium.
Ultrasonic sound is
above 20 kHz
, beyond human hearing.

secs.t: Ultrasound, infrasound, SONAR and echo · Revision points (11)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #19 (pp 76-81)
Ultrasound is used for medical imaging.
SONAR sends ultrasonic pulses, receives their echoes and uses the time interval to find distance.
SONAR uses ultrasound for underwater detection.
An echo is distinct if it returns after 0.1 s; at about 344 m/s sound travels 34.4 m, so the reflector must be at least
away.
Ultrasound is used in echocardiography.
Infrasound is used for earthquake detection.
All three apply: SONAR ultrasound has high frequency, so it diffracts less and travels as a narrow, directed beam.
SONAR is used to detect submarines.
SONAR measures ocean depth.
Medical ultrasound uses echoes to image internal organs.
Dolphins use echolocation for navigation.

secs.t: Musical instruments · Revision points (5)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #19 (pp 76-81)
String instruments produce sound through vibration of strings.
String instruments include the guitar, sitar, and violin.
The pitch of a musical instrument is controlled by the frequency of vibration.
The amplitude of vibration depends on the force of striking or blowing.
A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics.

secs.t: Nature of light and media · Revision points (7)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #18 (pp 64-76)
The
particle nature
of light explains the photoelectric effect.
Light exhibits wave nature.
All three are explained by the wave nature of light: interference, diffraction and polarisation.
Electromagnetic waves are transverse.
Light is fastest in a
vacuum
at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s and slows in air, water and glass as optical density rises.
A transparent medium allows light to pass through it.
A medium with a higher refractive index is
optically denser
, so light travels more slowly in it.

secs.t: Reflection and mirrors · Revision points (13)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #18 (pp 64-76)
The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence, not parallel.
A rough surface scatters rays in many directions, giving
irregular or diffused reflection
with no clear image.
A plane mirror is used in a periscope.
A plane mirror gives an image the same size and erect, so m = +1.
An object inside F of a concave mirror gives a virtual, erect, magnified image, not an inverted one.
A regular or specular reflection occurs from a smooth surface.
A plane mirror laterally inverts an image.
A plane mirror is used as a looking glass.
A concave mirror focuses sunlight at its focus in solar cookers and furnaces.
A shaving or makeup mirror produces a magnified erect image when the object is within F.
A convex mirror is used in street lamps.
A vehicle rear-view mirror produces an erect diminished image.
A reflecting telescope has a large aperture.

secs.t: Refraction, total internal reflection and optical fibres · Revision points (24)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #18 (pp 64-76)
Total internal reflection occurs when the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle for light travelling from a denser to a rarer medium.
Frequency stays the same while speed and wavelength change.
Lenses converge or diverge light.
An optical fibre keeps light inside its core.
Diamond brilliance results from multiple total internal reflections.
A Porro prism or binocular produces image inversion without loss.
Sunlight enters a drop, refracts and disperses, reflects totally inside the back of the drop, and refracts out, giving A, B, C, D.
Cameras form images using refraction.
TIR needs light going from denser to rarer medium beyond the critical angle, no refraction occurs, and ideally all the light is reflected.
The core of an optical fibre has a higher refractive index than its cladding.
Optical fibres are immune to interference.
Optical fibres transmit signals.
Optical fibres are used in medical endoscopy.
Optical-fibre sensors detect strain.
Optical fibres carry light for decorative and medical illumination.
An endoscope works through a bundle of optical fibres using total internal reflection.
An endoscope is flexible enough to be inserted into body cavities.
An inferior mirage occurs in a desert.
A mirage can appear as an inverted image of a distant object.
Diamond has a very high refractive index of approximately 2.42.
Diamond's critical angle is very small (about 24°), so most light inside meets the faces beyond it and is totally internally reflected, making it sparkle.
Prisms in binoculars or periscopes reflect light without silvering.
A mirage is caused by a continuous decrease or increase of refractive index with height.
The critical angle is the angle of incidence in a denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°.

secs.t: Lenses · Revision points (16)

x: Source:
Physics – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #18 (pp 64-76)
A concave lens is diverging; a convex lens is converging.
Lens power is measured in
dioptre
s; P = 1/f with f in metres.
A convex lens forms a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is within F.
Myopia is corrected with a concave lens of negative power, not positive.
Astigmatism is corrected with a cylindrical lens.
Concavo-convex (thicker centre) is a convex lens, while double-concave, plano-concave and convexo-concave are concave lenses.

D. Rutherford discovered nitrogen in 1772.
H. Cavendish distinguished hydrogen as a distinct gas.
Phosphorus came in 1669, hydrogen 1766, oxygen 1771 and nitrogen 1772, giving B, D, C, A.
Only fluorine is linked to Moissan.

G. Brandt discovered cobalt in 1735.
J. and F. Elhuyar discovered tungsten in 1783.

Scheele identified molybdenum in 1778, and Peter Jacob
Hjelm
later isolated the metal.

secs.t: National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) · Revision points (17)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #15 (pp 37-39)
The NDRF regional HQ for Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka is at
Vijayawada
(10th Battalion).
The NDRF was raised in 2006 under Section 44 of the DM Act, 2005.
NDRF has 16 battalions.
The NDRF is the response force, the NCMC coordinates crises, the Chief Secretary heads the State Crisis Committee, and the Collector heads district DM.
NDRF responds to floods.
The headquarters of NDRF is in New Delhi.
NDRF stands for
National Disaster Response Force
The community is the first responder in disasters.
NDRF Raising Day is 19 January, its motto 'Aapada Seva Sadaiv Sarvatra' means 'Disaster Service Always Everywhere', and it is the world's largest dedicated disaster force.
All five are part of NDRF teams: engineers, technicians, electricians, dog squads, and medical staff.
Each NDRF battalion has approximately 1,149 personnel.
NDRF personnel come on deputation from the BSF, CRPF, CISF, ITBP, SSB and Assam Rifles.
A is true: the NDRF is headed by a Director General drawn from the senior IPS cadre.
Each NDRF battalion has 18 self-contained search and rescue teams of about 45 people each.
CSSR stands for Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue, an NDRF speciality used after earthquakes and building collapses.
NDRF’s strategic placement is based on the vulnerability profile across India.
The NDRF went to Japan after the 2011 tsunami, Nepal after the 2015 earthquake, Turkey in 2023 under Operation Dost and Myanmar in 2025 under Operation Brahma.

secs.t: State Disaster Response Force · Revision points (7)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #21 (pp 49-50)
The State Disaster Response Force is the counterpart of the National Disaster Response Force.
The State Response Force rests on Section 44, the State Response Fund on Section 48(1)(a), the SEC administers the fund, and up to 10% may go to State-specific disasters.
The State Disaster Response Force is a state-level specialised response force.
The State Disaster Response Force is the first responder within the state.
All five supply SDRF personnel: State police, armed police, fire services, home guards and civil defence.
The SDRF uses a battalion model like the NDRF's, with multi-disciplinary teams.
CSSR is Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue, CBRN is Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear, MFR is Medical First Response, and the SDRF force is the State Disaster Response Force.

secs.t: State Disaster Response Fund · Revision points (6)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #21 (pp 49-50)
For general-category states, the Centre contributes 75% to the State Disaster Response Fund.
Frost and cold waves are on the notified list for SDRF help, along with cyclone, flood, drought and others.
The State Disaster Response Fund is the primary fund available with states for immediate relief.
The State Executive Committee, headed by
the Chief Secretary
, administers the State Disaster Response Fund.
All four are notified disasters for SDRF help: fire, pest attack, cyclone and drought.
The SDRF cannot be used to compensate individual losses.

secs.t: Mitigation measures and mitigation funds · Revision points (18)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #12 (pp 30-32)
Under the DM Act, mitigation means measures to reduce the risk, impact or effects of a disaster or threatening disaster.
Andhra Pradesh's most cyclone-prone stretch is Ongole–Machilipatnam.
Mitigation is the most cost-effective phase of the Disaster Management Cycle.
Floods are met with embankments and dams, cyclones with coastal embankments and shelters, droughts with check dams and farm ponds, and landslides with retaining walls.
The key mitigation funds are the National Disaster Mitigation Fund and the State Disaster Mitigation Fund.
Structural mitigation consists of physical or engineering constructions.
Risk assessment is general mitigation, building guidelines are for earthquakes, flood-plain management for floods, and controlling settlement in hazard areas for landslides.
Flood-proofing is a flood mitigation measure.
Prevention, mitigation and preparedness belong to the pre-disaster phase.
The disaster-management paradigm has shifted from relief-centric management to mitigation-centric management.
All three are structural mitigation: quake-resistant buildings, retrofitting and sea walls.
All nine are non-structural mitigation: building codes (IS 1893, National Building Code), flood-plain zoning, land-use planning, insurance, awareness, early warning and training.
The Central Water Commission is associated with flood forecasting.
Seismic microzonation is a non-structural earthquake-mitigation measure.
Coastal regulation zones are non-structural cyclone-mitigation measures.
Three are non-structural for drought: drought-resistant crops, water conservation and PMFBY insurance.
Mainstreaming Disaster Risk Reduction is part of the Prime Minister's 10-Point Agenda.
Afforestation
is a non-structural landslide measure.

secs.t: Earthquakes — basics and seismic zones · Revision points (9)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #10 (pp 25-27), #4 (pp 10-14)
John Milne
, who built an early horizontal seismograph, is called the father of modern seismology.
Under IS 1893:2016, Zone III (moderate, intensity VII) has a zone factor of 0.16, not 0.24.
The focus is the underground origin, the epicentre lies directly above it, intensity is measured on the Mercalli scale, and the IS 1893:2016 map has four zones, II to V.
An earthquake is a geological disaster.
Andhra Pradesh lies in Zones II and III, Zone V includes the North-East and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Delhi is in Zone IV, and the stable peninsular shield is mostly Zone II.
Seismic Zone II covers most of Peninsular India, which is a stable region.
A tsunami is a natural disaster.
The focus is where a quake starts, the epicentre is the point above it, the Mercalli scale measures intensity, and the seismograph records shaking.
An earthquake beneath the sea can cause a tsunami.

secs.t: Major Indian earthquakes and seismic management · Revision points (10)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #10 (pp 25-27)
The Bhuj earthquake occurred in Gujarat in 2001.
NCS gives real-time quake monitoring, NDMA sets policy guidelines, IS 1893 covers quake-resistant design, and NDRF does specialist search and rescue.
The Assam quake struck in 1897, Kangra 1905, Bihar–Nepal 1934 and Assam–Tibet 1950.
The 1897 Assam quake (8.1) was among the first well-studied great quakes, and the 1905 Kangra quake (7.8) killed about 20,000 people.
The 1934 Bihar–Nepal quake (8.1) devastated the Gangetic plains, and the 1950 Assam–Tibet quake (8.6) was one of the largest ever recorded.
The Koyna earthquake occurred in 1967.
The Latur or Killari earthquake occurred in 1993.
Latur (1993) killed about 10,000, Bhuj (2001) was 7.7, Sikkim (2011) 6.9, and Nepal–Gorkha (2015) 7.8.
The Sikkim earthquake affected the Himalayan region.
The National Building Code incorporates seismic provisions.

secs.t: Tsunamis · Revision points (14)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #4 (pp 10-14)
A tsunami is a series of large waves caused by a sudden movement of the sea floor that displaces a huge volume of water.
The International Tsunami Information Centre is in Honolulu.
Remote sensing, GIS and satellite data are used to map tsunami and coastal risk.
The order is the International Day for DR (1989), the IDNDR decade (1990), the Yokohama conference (1994) and Sendai (2015).
All five were badly hit by the 2004 tsunami: Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Kerala, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Tsunamis are most commonly associated with earthquakes.
A tsunami can strike at
any time of day or night
, as it depends on sea-floor movement, not time or season.
All four are tsunami effects: stripping beaches, uprooting plantations, flooding far inland, and damaging life and property.
As a tsunami nears shallow water it slows down and grows much taller.
Tsunami waves reach coastal areas.
The Indian Ocean tsunami struck on 26
December 2004
, after a 9.1 quake off Sumatra.
The tsunami struck on 26 December 2004, about 5,640 people in India remained unaccounted for, and damage was estimated at over ₹11,000 crore, about US$2.56 billion.
The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre is abbreviated as ITEWC.
Tsunami Day is 5 November, the DRR Day 13 October, Sendai is about disaster risk reduction, and GIS works with spatial data.

secs.t: Disaster scales and intensity measures · Revision points (9)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #9 (pp 24-25)
The International Nuclear Event Scale (IAEA, 1990) rates nuclear and radiological events from 0 to 7.
The Beaufort scale rates wind force from 0 to 12.
The Moment Magnitude Scale is the modern standard.
Saffir-Simpson rates hurricane winds, Fujita tornadoes, Richter quake energy, and Beaufort general wind force.
The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale is used for cyclones in India.
Fujita runs F0/EF0 to F5/EF5, Richter was devised in 1935, moment magnitude is written Mw, and the Modified Mercalli scale is MMI.
Fujita rates tornadoes, and the Richter and moment magnitude scales are logarithmic, Richter usually running from 1 to 10.
Earthquake intensity on the Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is based on observed effects and damage.
The MSK-64 intensity scale is used in India and much of Europe.

secs.t: Tropical cyclones and hurricanes · Revision points (18)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #6 (pp 16-19), #14 (pp 34-37)
The IMD forecasts cyclones in India.
India does not get hurricanes.
Hurricanes are rated on the Saffir-Simpson scale, tornadoes on the Fujita scale, typhoons hit the north-west Pacific, and cyclones the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.
Category 1 hurricanes have wind speeds of 119–153 km/h.
A hurricane is a large, rotating tropical storm system.
Hurricanes form over
warm ocean waters
, usually at least 26–27°C, which supply their heat and moisture.
A hurricane has a low-pressure centre called the eye.
A hurricane rotates counter-clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.
All four are hurricane regions: the North and Central Atlantic, the Caribbean, the Gulf of Mexico and the north-east Pacific.
The north-west Pacific, home of typhoons, covers
East Asia, the Philippines and Japan
Category 2 hurricanes have wind speeds of 154–177 km/h.
In India a tropical
cyclone
is simply called a cyclone. 'Hurricane' and 'typhoon' are used elsewhere.
All five are cyclone threats: high winds, storm surge, heavy rain, flooding and coastal inundation.
A cyclone produces heavy rainfall.
A cyclone is a rapid-onset disaster.
The East Coast is more vulnerable to cyclones than the West Coast.
The Bay of Bengal to Arabian Sea cyclone ratio is approximately 4:1.
Tornado wind speeds can exceed 300 km/h in severe cases.

secs.t: IMD cyclone classification · Revision points (8)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #14 (pp 34-37), #30 (pp 65-66)
An IMD depression has wind speed of 31–49 km/h.
A low-pressure area is below 31 km/h, a deep depression 50–61 km/h, and a severe cyclonic storm 89–117 km/h.
The IMD starts naming systems at the
cyclonic storm
stage, from 62 km/h.
A very severe cyclonic storm is 118–166 km/h.
The maximum sustained wind speed is measured as a 3-minute average.
A low-pressure area is below 31 km/h, a depression 31–49, a deep depression 50–61, and a cyclonic storm 62–88 km/h.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) officially classifies low-pressure systems over the North Indian Ocean.
A
Low Pressure Area
is the weakest system.

secs.t: Cyclone agencies, projects and major cyclones · Revision points (15)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #6 (pp 16-19), #14 (pp 34-37)
The IMD is headquartered in New
Delhi
, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
The National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project is abbreviated as NCRMP.
In Andhra Pradesh the most cyclone-prone stretch is
Ongole to Machilipatnam
SCATSAT-1
, ISRO's scatterometer satellite, measures ocean-surface winds and helps predict and track cyclones.
Storm surge and high-wave warnings come from INCOIS.
A Doppler Radar Network forecasts heavy rainfall and thunderstorms.
The IMD forecasts, tracks and names cyclones, INCOIS warns of surge and high waves, NDMA sets policy, and NDRF/SDRF evacuate and rescue.
The order is Bhola (1970), the 1977 AP cyclone, Phailin (2013) and Hudhud (2014).
Phethai made landfall in Andhra Pradesh in December 2018.
APSDMA handles mitigation and response in AP, NCRMP early warning, NDMA policy and coordination, and INCOIS surge and wave warnings.
NCRMP gives early warning, and the 1999 Odisha super cyclone killed about 10,000 people and spurred modern disaster management.
Phailin led to massive evacuation.
Hudhud (2014) badly damaged Visakhapatnam, Fani (2019) hit Odisha with a model evacuation of about 1.2 million, and Amphan (2020) hit West Bengal.
Tauktae was a rare intense west-coast cyclone.
Cyclone forecasting in India is conducted by the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD).

secs.t: Tornadoes · Revision points (9)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #5 (pp 14-16)
Tornadoes are rated on the
Fujita scale
, now in its Enhanced Fujita form.
Tornadoes in India peak before the monsoon, March to May, with the nor'westers (Kal Baisakhi).
A tornado looks like a funnel cloud, lasts a few minutes, moves at up to about 90–100 km/h, and has winds of 105–322 km/h.
A tornado is a violently rotating column of air that extends from a thunderstorm to the ground.
The Enhanced Fujita scale has six categories, EF0 to EF5.
The Belda tornado struck on 24 March 1998, New Delhi in 1978, Berhampore in 1993 and Kendrapara in 2009.
A tornado funnel can be narrow or wide.
All four have seen recent tornadoes: Odisha, Punjab, Haryana, and Jammu and Kashmir.
The 1998 Belda tornado killed about 250 people.

secs.t: Floods — nature, types and extent · Revision points (10)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #11 (pp 27-30), #19 (pp 45-47)
A flood is water overflowing onto land that is normally dry, from heavy rain, rivers bursting their banks, or other causes.
The Rashtriya Barh Ayog put the flood-prone area at about 40 million hectares.
Riverine or fluvial floods result from the overflow of rivers due to heavy monsoon rainfall.
Flood water flows in rivers, streams, and other water bodies and cannot be contained.
Floods are India's most frequent disaster and cause huge yearly losses of money, lives and crops.
All four basins see river floods: the Ganga, Brahmaputra, Kosi and Godavari.
Flash floods result from sudden intense rainfall or cloudbursts.
Mumbai commonly experiences urban floods.
The west coast commonly experiences coastal floods.
Heavy rain can cause flooding, prolonged rain landslides, landslides can block rivers and cause havoc downstream, and poor drainage worsens urban floods.

secs.t: Flood management and major floods · Revision points (8)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #11 (pp 27-30), #19 (pp 45-47)
GIS deals with spatial data.
The National Flood Commission was established in 1980.
The CWC runs flood forecasting, NDMA sets policy, the Brahmaputra Board controls floods and erosion in the North-East, and NDRF/SDRF rescue and give relief.
The order is Mumbai (2005), Kedarnath (2013), Chennai (2015) and Kerala (2018).
Odisha made the flood hazard atlas, based on satellite images of past floods from 2000 to 2018, to manage floods better.
The Rashtriya Barh Ayog recommended comprehensive flood management.
Bihar experienced a major flood in 2008.
NDMA's flood guidelines came in 2008 and its urban flooding guidelines in 2010, the Odisha atlas covers 2000–2018, and the Rashtriya Barh Ayog, set up in 1976, reported in 1980.

secs.t: Cloudbursts · Revision points (12)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #19 (pp 45-47)
The IMD defines a cloudburst as at least 100 mm of rain in one hour over about 20–30 sq km.
Cloudbursts usually happen at 1,000–2,500 m in mountains, not 500–1,000 m.
A cloudburst is a highly localised extreme weather event.
Orographic lifting pushes moist air up slopes, instability builds tall cumulonimbus clouds, monsoon air supplies moisture, and the water falls all at once when updrafts weaken.
Flood management includes flood forecasting, warnings, and disaster preparedness.
A cloudburst is a rapid-onset disaster, striking within minutes to hours.
A cloudburst can trigger flash floods.
Cloudbursts occasionally occur in plains, although such events are rare.
Two are the main secondary hazards of cloudbursts: flash floods and landslides.
Doppler radar detects intense rain cells in real time, nowcasting gives forecasts for the next few hours, orographic lifting forces moist air up slopes, and the cumulonimbus cloud releases the burst.
The Leh cloudburst was in 2010.
A hailstorm is precipitation in the form of ice pellets called hailstones.

secs.t: Hailstorms · Revision points (5)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #16 (pp 39-41)
Hailstorms in India occur mainly before the monsoon (March–May) and in winter, not October–December, and are rare in the monsoon.
Maharashtra's hail areas are Vidarbha and Marathwada, central India's MP and Chhattisgarh, the north-west's Punjab to Himachal, and others include Bihar, Karnataka and Uttarakhand.
A hailstorm is not biological, an earthquake strikes suddenly (rapid-onset), drought is slow-onset, and climate change is making extreme convective events more frequent.
Strong updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds freeze raindrops during hailstorm formation.
Convective instability, moisture and updrafts are atmospheric factors, western disturbances are synoptic factors, and plateaus and hills boost convection.

secs.t: Drought — nature, causes and history · Revision points (8)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #8 (pp 22-24)
Drought is a long shortage of rain or moisture that leads to water scarcity.
The DM Act was passed in 2005, not 2006.
About 68% of India is drought-prone, rain-fed farming makes it vulnerable, and peninsular surface water runs short in poor-rain years.
Three sectors are hit by drought: agriculture, drinking water and industry.
The order is the Arthashastra (4th century BC), relief works after Independence, the Green Revolution (late 1960s) and the DM Act (2005).
Drought is a slow-onset disaster.
Uneven and inadequate rain is the main cause, over 80% of rain falls in under 100 monsoon days, and overusing groundwater worsens drought over time.
Chronically drought-prone areas get under 750 mm of rain and cover about 33% of India; drought-prone areas get 750–1125 mm and cover about 35%.

secs.t: Drought — types, indicators and management · Revision points (7)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #8 (pp 22-24)
The 2016 Manual for Drought Management adopted a multi-indicator approach rather than relying only on rainfall.
Meteorological drought is indicated by a rainfall deficiency of at least 25% from the long-period average.
NDMA's drought guidelines came in 2010, the Drought Manual was revised in 2016, the SDRF is the first relief fund, and the NDRF is used in severe cases.
Meteorological drought shows up at once, agricultural after a short lag, hydrological after weeks to months, and socio-economic after a long lag.
Agricultural drought occurs when soil moisture is insufficient for crop growth.
All five are drought indicators: rainfall deviation, dry spells, NDVI (vegetation index), soil moisture, and reservoir and groundwater levels.
MGNREGA provides employment support in drought management.

secs.t: Heatwaves · Revision points (13)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #33 (pp 70-72)
The IMD forecasts heatwaves.
A heatwave means temperatures well above the normal maximum, not below.
Heatwave is a notified disaster.
Green means no action, yellow means stay updated, orange means be prepared, and red means take action.
A heatwave needs at least 40°C in the plains, 37°C on the coast, and 30°C in the hills.
NDMA's guidelines for heatwave action plans are the key document.
A heatwave in plains is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C to 6.4°C.
In the plains, an actual maximum of 45°C or more counts as a heatwave, and 47°C or more as a severe heatwave.
States and cities
prepare heat action plans with help from NDMA and the IMD.
Cool roofs use reflective coatings or white paint to keep buildings cooler.
All three are public-awareness measures: sharing dos and don'ts, distributing ORS, and opening cooling centres.
Structural measures include shade structures.
The IMD forecasts, NDMA issued the 2021 cold wave guidelines, early warning uses colour codes, and frost protection is the farm measure.

secs.t: Cold waves · Revision points (10)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #34 (pp 72-74)
NDMA's guidelines on cold waves and frost came in 2021, not 2022.
Homeless people are among the groups most vulnerable to cold waves.
In the plains 4°C or below is a cold wave and 2°C or below a severe one, and coastal stations use a 15°C threshold.
A cold wave is a sharp drop in minimum temperature below normal in winter.
The minimum-temperature threshold for declaring a cold wave in plains is 10°C or below.
The coastal cold-wave rule is 15°C or below with a departure of 4.5°C or more, and cold and severe cold days are judged by how far the maximum falls below normal.
All four are health effects of cold waves: hypothermia, respiratory illness, frostbite, and more deaths among the elderly and children.
Cold waves affect livestock.
NDMA's cold wave guidelines focus on preparedness, mapping vulnerability and community awareness.
Protective measures against cold waves include medical preparedness.

secs.t: Landslides — nature, triggers and regions · Revision points (20)

x: Source:
Disaster Management – ROCKET Sheets PDF, ROCKET SHEET #18 (pp 43-45)
A landslide is the mass movement of rock, debris or earth down a slope or riverbank under gravity.
NDMA's guidelines on landslides and snow avalanches came in 2009, not 2019.
The National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping programme is conducted by the Geological Survey of India (GSI).

The north-west Himalaya's slides come from quakes, rain and road cutting; the north-east's from rain and jhum farming; the Western Ghats' from monsoon rain and deforestation; and the Eastern Ghats' from local heavy rain.
Retaining walls are structural, hazard zonation maps non-structural, and hill building codes regulatory.
Approximately 12.6% of India’s land area is landslide-prone.
Landslides may occur gradually or suddenly without warning.
The Himalayas are among the most vulnerable regions to landslides in India.
Controlling settlement in hazard-prone areas reduces landslide risk.
A landslide is a hydro-meteorological hazard.
The National Landslide Risk Management Strategy was issued in 2019.
Three are in the north-west Himalaya: J&K, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
Six are in the north-east Himalaya: Sikkim, Arunachal, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland and Meghalaya.
Five are in the Western Ghats and Konkan: Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Goa and the Nilgiris.
All four are structural landslide measures: rock bolting, wire mesh, better drainage and slope grading.
All three are non-structural landslide measures: early warning, land-use rules and awareness.
GSI set up the
National Landslide Forecasting Centre
to issue regional landslide forecasts.
In high-risk landslide zones, building should be restricted.
NDMA guidelines provide for structural avalanche mitigation measures.
The DGRE issues daily avalanche warning bulletins during the winter season.

secs.t: Avalanches · Revision points (14)

x: Source:

An avalanche is a rapid flow of snow, ice and debris down a mountain slope.
The Ministry of Defence is the nodal ministry for avalanches, with DGRE (formerly SASE) as the technical agency.
The key technical agency for avalanche management is the Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment (DGRE).
A slab avalanche is a large snow slab breaking off, a loose-snow avalanche is a small dry slide, an ice avalanche comes from glaciers, and a debris avalanche mixes rock, soil and snow.
Heavy snowfall is a natural cause of avalanches.
The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) constructs roads in avalanche-prone areas.
An avalanche is a geological and snow-related natural hazard.
The
slab avalanche
, where a large block of snow breaks away, is the most dangerous type.
All five are natural causes: weak snow layers, slopes of 30–45°, earthquakes, sudden warming and rain on snow.
All three are human or other causes: road building, deforestation and climate change.
J&K is the worst affected, Ladakh has high-altitude avalanche zones, Lahaul-Spiti and Kinnaur are in Himachal Pradesh, and the high Garhwal and Kumaon Himalaya are in Uttarakhand.
Rohtang and Chamba (Himachal), the high Garhwal and Kumaon (Uttarakhand), and the high stretches of Sikkim and Arunachal are avalanche-prone.
All three are DGRE activities: avalanche forecasting, research and hazard mapping.
The DGRE develops avalanche mitigation technologies.

The Fukushima Daiichi disaster, set off by a tsunami, happened in 2011, not 2010, and was rated INES Level 7.
A nuclear disaster is a man-made or technological disaster.
A nuclear explosion is not a natural disaster.

The CCS handles nuclear, biological and chemical emergencies, nuclear disasters involve reactors, radiological ones involve orphan sources, transport or dirty bombs, and the main threat is ionising radiation.
Ionising radiation includes alpha radiation, beta radiation, gamma radiation and neutrons.
Nuclear disasters can cause cancer and genetic damage, and contaminate the environment for decades or centuries.
The Mayapuri incident was a radiological emergency.
Chernobyl was in 1986 (Ukraine, the worst accident), Fukushima in 2011 (tsunami), Three Mile Island in 1979 (USA, partial meltdown), and Mayapuri in 2010 (Delhi, Cobalt-60).

GIS is a
Geographic Information System
, used to store, analyse and present spatial data.
GIS is used for evacuation route planning during preparedness.
Tsunami inundation modelling is done by INCOIS.
GIS maps flood inundation, models cyclone storm surges, assesses farm drought (NADAMS), and models tsunami inundation and evacuation.
GIS is used for hazard zonation mapping during prevention or mitigation.
Disaster mapping uses remote sensing, GIS and satellite data; advanced GIS models spatial data, shows community vulnerability, and stores, analyses and presents geographic data.
All three are prevention-phase GIS uses: vulnerability assessment, risk mapping and land-use planning.
Hazard zonation is a prevention or mitigation use of GIS, evacuation route planning a preparedness use, search and rescue coordination a response use, and monitoring reconstruction a recovery use.
GIS supports flood zoning and monitoring, cyclone tracking and evacuation, quake zoning and damage mapping, and landslide work.
For forest fires, GIS detects and monitors fires.
ISRO has a Disaster Management Support Programme.
NDMA uses GIS for planning, decision support and drafting guidelines.
SDMAs use GIS for developing guidelines.
NDEM
is the National Database for Emergency Management.
